claims.text: This is a classic yoshoku (Japanese Western) kitchen and is not celiac-safe. The signature dishes are wheat-heavy by design: the hand-kneaded hamburger relies on a flour-and-wine demi-glace, and fried items like fried shrimp, cream croquettes, tonkatsu and chicken nanban are breaded/floured. Fryer oil is almost certainly shared among breaded foods.
No gluten-free menu or allergen accommodation is documented on the restaurant's website or in available sources. Guests with celiac disease should not assume any dish is safe.

Japanese yoshoku seasoning here leans on soy-based sauces and dashi; one documented special is an avocado hamburger steak with wasabi soy sauce. Standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so soy-seasoned dishes should be treated as containing both soy and wheat.

The menu is centered on meat (hamburger steak, tonkatsu, chicken nanban, ginger pork) and fried seafood, with no vegan options documented. Sauces and seasonings rely on meat-based demi-glace and dashi, so cross-contact with animal products throughout the kitchen should be assumed.

Rice is freshly milled in-house each day and plain white rice is served with free refills, which can be a naturally gluten-free, low-allergen staple if prepared and served separately from sauced dishes (confirm with staff).

This is a charcoal yakitori (grilled chicken skewer) restaurant. Standard yakitori is glazed with a tare made from soy sauce and mirin, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the skewers and sauces should be assumed to contain gluten. No gluten-free preparation is documented on any source.
Raw chicken preparations (chicken sashimi, tori no otsukuri) are typically served with soy-based dipping sauces, another likely source of wheat-containing soy.

Soy sauce and tare are central to a yakitori menu like this one, and most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat. A celiac diner should not assume any skewer, dipping sauce, or finishing dish is wheat-free here.

This is a chicken-focused omakase counter (skewers, raw chicken, meatballs); the menu is built entirely around chicken with no vegan course documented. Shared charcoal grill and dashi/soy seasonings make cross-contact with animal products unavoidable.
The restaurant asks guests to share any allergies, disliked ingredients, or special requests at the time of reservation, so it is worth contacting them directly in advance to discuss needs.

Reservations invite advance notice of allergies and dislikes, and reviewers consistently praise the owner and staff for attentive, careful hospitality, suggesting they will engage seriously if you raise dietary concerns ahead of time.

name: 京おでん だいすけ (Kyo-Oden Daisuke)

claims.text: This is dashi-and-oden cooking and is not celiac-safe. Oden items such as abura-age (fried tofu) and various fishcakes and simmered items commonly contain wheat and soy, and everything cooks together in shared simmering pots, so cross-contact is unavoidable.
No gluten-free menu or allergen program is documented at this restaurant.
The broth and seasonings rely on fish-sauce and soy-based seasonings (including Noto ishiru); typical Japanese soy sauce and related seasonings contain wheat, which is pervasive in oden cooking here.

Not vegan-friendly: the foundational dashi is built on katsuobushi (bonito), niboshi (sardines), and ishiru (fish sauce), so even vegetable items like daikon or potato are simmered in fish-based broth.

name: 京都 下町のお好み焼き 昌・べた焼きの専門店 (Kyoto Shitamachi no Okonomiyaki Masa (Be)

claims.text: This is a betayaki (Kyoto-style okonomiyaki) specialist. The core dish is built on a wheat-flour batter cooked on a shared griddle (teppan), so it is not celiac-safe. Gluten is central to virtually every dish here.
Everything is cooked together on a single shared teppan (griddle), so cross-contact with wheat batter is unavoidable. No gluten-free preparation is documented.
Okonomiyaki/betayaki sauce is wheat- and soy-based, and most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat. There is no indication of a wheat-free or soy-free sauce option here.

Betayaki batter and toppings commonly include egg, and the menu features meat and pork-offal items (oil cas/aburakasu, beef, horumon). The single shared griddle cooks animal products, so vegan diners face heavy cross-contact. No vegan options are documented; confirm directly.

This is a chuka soba (ramen) shop whose core dishes are built on wheat: the chuka soba uses wheat ramen noodles, and the menu also includes udon and soba. The kitchen is wheat-centric, so flour and wheat-noodle traces are essentially unavoidable. Not suitable for celiacs.

The signature broth is a light shoyu (soy sauce) base with Japanese dashi. Standard Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the broth itself should be assumed to contain wheat in addition to the noodles.

The broth is built on Japanese dashi (typically bonito/fish-based) and soy sauce, and dishes are served with meat such as braised beef tendon, so the menu is not vegan and animal-based stock is central to the cooking.

This is a wheat- and soy-heavy町中華 (Chinese diner): the core menu is gyoza (wheat dumpling wrappers), ramen (wheat noodles), tenshinhan and wok dishes built on soy sauce and wheat/soy-based seasonings. It is not celiac-safe, and cross-contamination risk is high.
Gyoza is offered pan-fried, boiled, and deep-fried, and dishes are cooked in shared woks and a busy, fast-turnover kitchen — there is no documented gluten-free preparation or separation.
Signature dishes such as the tenshinhan rely on a heavily seasoned soy-based sauce; most Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat, so these dishes should be assumed to contain gluten.

No vegan or vegetarian menu is documented. The kitchen centers on pork gyoza, egg, wagyu beef and other meat dishes cooked in shared woks, so cross-contact with animal products should be expected. Vegan diners should confirm directly with staff.

This is a katsudon and udon/soba shokudo built around wheat: the signature pork cutlet is breaded in wheat flour and panko, and the kitchen also serves wheat udon noodles, fried croquettes, breaded minced cutlets, and hamburger. Shared frying oil and shared cooking surfaces make gluten cross-contamination essentially unavoidable. This is not a celiac-safe restaurant.
Even the rice-bowl dishes are not gluten-free: the katsudon's egg-and-onion binding sauce is a dashi-and-soy-based broth, and the cutlet itself is wheat-breaded.

The katsudon, donburi, udon and soba here all rely on soy-and-dashi-based sauces and broths. As with virtually all Japanese shokudo, the soy sauce almost certainly contains wheat, so these dishes should be treated as containing gluten.

There is no vegan offering here. The menu centers on pork cutlet, egg, beef, and shrimp, and the udon/soba broths are dashi-based (typically bonito/fish stock). Even simpler dishes would carry animal-derived dashi and egg, so cross-contact with animal products is pervasive throughout the kitchen.

This is a wheat-heavy kissaten built around toast, bread, and breaded fried teishoku (hire katsu pork cutlets, croquettes, fried shrimp). Wheat is pervasive across the menu and there is no documented gluten-free accommodation, so cross-contamination should be assumed. Not celiac-safe.
Signature items such as the potato croquette toast sandwich and the breaded hire katsu and fried shrimp sets all involve breadcrumbs and bread, sharing prep and frying surfaces with wheat.

Lunch teishoku come with miso soup and Japanese sides, and the hamburg is finished in a demi-glace sauce; soy sauce and dashi are typical in this style of cooking and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. Treat the set meals as containing wheat-based seasonings.

No vegan options are documented. The menu centers on meat (hamburg, pork cutlet), seafood (fried shrimp, shrimp butter rice), eggs, ham, cheese, butter, and dashi-based dishes, so vegan dining is not realistically accommodated and cross-contact with animal products is unavoidable.
